claims.text: Superconductivity in the high-entropy alloy is governed by its electronic structure.
Superconductivity in the high-entropy alloy is governed by the robustness of its crystal structure against lattice compression.
Scanning tunneling microscopy or spectroscopy can probe the alloy's electronic structure and superconducting properties.
The starting material is a high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior is uncharacterized.
Scanning tunneling microscopy or spectroscopy will be used to characterize the material's electronic structure and superconducting properties.
The test will be conducted at low temperature.
The relevant structural mediator is the alloy's crystal structure.
Robustness of the crystal structure against lattice compression enables superconductivity to emerge.
The selected high-entropy alloy will exhibit superconductivity with a critical temperature close to 7.5 K.
The baseline is a non-superconducting state of the same high-entropy alloy.
The hypothesis is intended to hold between 1 K and 10 K.
The exact relationship between electronic structure and the emergence of superconductivity is not fully understood.
A critical temperature not close to 7.5 K would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as an 'uncharacterized superconducting state,' while the baseline is declared non-superconducting; the relationship between these two starting-state descriptions is not resolved.

The intervention only measures the material by microscopy or spectroscopy, whereas the proposed mechanism concerns response to lattice compression; no compression or pressure perturbation is included.
